1.title: Protecting the Main Branch
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Protecting the Main Branch. It covers the exam area Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Explain why main is protected. Set up required reviews and status checks. Choose between branch protection rules and rulesets. Use linear history, signed commits, merge queue and auto-merge. Write a code owners file. Read a rejected push. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Course
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the course. Part: Part four: Git Hub collaboration. Verified with: Git two point five zero.one for the local parts; the Git Hub documentation (read twenty twenty-six-eleven to sixteen) for the Git Hub parts.

1.title: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only
1.text: What Was Executed and What Is Reference Only. Protection rules run on Git Hub and cannot be run locally: the settings come from the official Git Hub documentation. The local demonstration with a push hook is only a model of the idea.

1.title: Why protect main, and what a rule can require
1.text: Why protect main, and what a rule can require. Main is what the whole team builds and deploys from, so one careless push hurts everyone. Protection forces every change through a pull request, a review and green checks. The figure shows the gates between a branch and main.

1.title: Why protect main, and what a rule can require, continued
1.text: Why protect main, and what a rule can require. The figure shows this: Gates between a feature branch and main: pull request, required reviews, required status checks, then merge, with direct pushes to main blocked.

1.title: Why protect main, and what a rule can require, continued
1.text: Why protect main, and what a rule can require. A branch protection rule targets one branch, all branches or a name pattern. By default each rule blocks force pushes and deletion. Admins are exempt unless you turn on "Do not allow bypassing the above settings".

1.title: Why protect main, and what a rule can require, continued
1.text: Why protect main, and what a rule can require. Require pull request reviews before merging. The approvals you set. Require status checks before merging. The named checks must succeed. Require conversation resolution before merging. Every review thread resolved. Require signed commits. Every commit carries a verified signature. Require linear history. No merge commits; squash or ree base merging must be enabled. Require merge queue. P Rs merge through a queue. Lock branch. Read-only, and it cannot be deleted. Restrict who can push to matching branches. Only the people or apps you list.

1.title: Why protect main, and what a rule can require, continued
1.text: Why protect main, and what a rule can require. The review options add three switches: "Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed", "Require review from Code Owners" and "Require approval of the most recent reviewable push". For status checks, "Require branches to be up to date before merging" is the strict mode and the default once checks are required. Three traps follow. The check name must match the job name. A workflow skipped by a filter leaves its required check Pending, so the P R waits forever. For the merge queue, the workflow must also listen to the merge group event.

1.title: Why protect main, and what a rule can require, continued
1.text: Why protect main, and what a rule can require. Two facts about signing: commits made in the web interface are signed by Git Hub's own key, but commits created by Rebase and merge are not signed by Git Hub. Tip: A required check is only as good as its trigger. Make sure the workflow runs on every P R, or the check can stay Pending.

1.text: A local model: the push that gets rejected. Real protection runs on Git Hub's servers, not in your clone. The demo builds only a model: a pre receive hook in a bare repository that refuses every update of main. Make the hook executable with chmod plus x. Install it after main exists. Try it. Switch on the model, then push to main.

1.title: Rules or rulesets
1.text: Rules or rulesets. Rulesets are an alternative to branch protection rules. The documentation calls them more flexible and says they have advantages, but it does not call them the recommended choice. How many apply. Branch protection rule: Only one rule per branch. Ruleset: Several at once; rules aggregate and the most restrictive version wins. Targets. Branch protection rule: A branch, all branches or a pattern. Ruleset: Branches or tags, by pattern. Exemptions. Branch protection rule: Admins are exempt unless the setting for admins is on. Ruleset: Roles, teams or Git Hub Apps can be exempted.

1.title: Rules or rulesets, continued
1.text: Rules or rulesets. A ruleset can be Active or Disabled without deleting it, and anyone with read access can view active rulesets. The limits are seventy-five per repository and seventy-five organization-wide, tied to the Team and Enterprise plans. Rulesets also layer with branch protection rules. Push rulesets (private and internal repositories) block pushes by file path, path length, file extension or file size.

1.title: Merge queue, auto-merge and CODEOWNERS
1.text: Merge queue, auto-merge and code owners. A merge queue merges P Rs into a busy protected branch after the required checks succeed. It tests each P R against the latest target branch plus the P Rs ahead of it, and the buttons read "Merge when ready" and "Confirm merge when ready". C I can be Git Hub Actions or another provider. Check the plan requirements for your account. Auto-merge is switched on with "Allow auto-merge" in Settings, General, Pull Requests. It appears only on P Rs that cannot merge yet, and it is disabled if someone without write access pushes to the P R.

2.title: Merge queue, auto-merge and CODEOWNERS, continued
2.text: Merge queue, auto-merge and code owners. A code owners file names who must review which paths. It lives in dot github slash, the root or docs slash (the first one found, in that order), and it must be on the P R's base branch. Patterns work like dot git ignore, and the last matching line wins. Owners are at username, at org slash team name or an email, need write access, and sit on one line. Invalid lines are skipped, paths are case-sensitive, and the file stays under three megabytes. Try it. This file has five lines. The demo asks Git's own ignore matcher which lines match and keeps the last.

2.title: Merge queue, auto-merge and CODEOWNERS, continued
2.text: Merge queue, auto-merge and code owners. src or app.js. Owner: @shop or frontend. Why: dot js is later than. docs or app.js. Owner: @shop or docs. Why: Both match; the later line wins. payments or charge.py. Owner: @shop or payments, @ada. Why: Two owners on one line. src or docs or x.md. Owner: @shop or maintainers. Why: The leading slash anchors slash docs slash to the root. To make owners mandatory, enable "Require review from Code Owners" in a rule or a ruleset. Approval from any one listed owner is enough. For a P R from a fork, Git Hub reads the base branch's file. Protect the file itself with an entry for slash dot github slash code owners. Tip: Order code owners from general to specific. Because the last match wins, a broad line placed at the end overrides every line above it.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Ada pushes her local main straight to the protected main and sees "remote rejected". What should she do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Move her commit to a branch, push it and open a pull request. Protection sends all changes through a branch and a pull request, and a force push is blocked too.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A required check named build stays Pending on a docs-only P R, because the workflow has a filter that skips docs changes. Why can the P R not merge? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: A workflow skipped by a filter leaves its required check Pending. The check never reports, so the merge box keeps waiting for it.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. An admin merged a P R without the required approval, because admins are exempt by default. Which setting closes that gap? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Do not allow bypassing the above settings. That setting applies the rules to admins as well.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A code owners file lists dot js at shop slash frontend and later slash docs slash at shop slash docs. Bob changes docs slash app dot js. Who owns the change? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: @shop or docs, because the last matching line wins. Both lines match, and the last matching pattern wins.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. An organization and a repository each want their own rules on main, and both must apply at the same time. Which feature allows that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Rulesets, which layer and apply the most restrictive version. Only one branch protection rule applies at a time, while several rulesets can apply together.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. "Require linear history" is on. Which merge methods can the team still use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Squash and ree base, because neither adds a merge commit. Linear history needs squash or ree base merging, which add no merge commit.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does a branch protection rule block by default? Answer: Force pushes and deletion of the branch. Question two. Where can the code owners file live? Answer: In dot github slash, the root or docs slash. Question three. Which workflow event must be listened to for the merge queue? Answer: merge group.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which check setting is the strict mode? Answer: "Require branches to be up to date before merging". Question five. How many branch protection rules apply to one branch at a time? Answer: One. Question six. Why is the pre-receive hook in the demo only a model? Answer: Real protection runs on Git Hub's servers.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Why: every change goes through a P R, review and checks. Defaults: a rule blocks force pushes and deletion. Reviews: dismiss stale approvals; require Code Owners; approve the most recent push. Status checks: name matches the job; skipped workflow means Pending; strict means up to date. History and signing: linear history needs squash or ree base; web commits signed by Git Hub, ree base merges not. Rules versus rulesets: one rule per branch; rulesets layer, most restrictive wins, limits of seventy-five, exempt list. Merge queue: tests P Rs in order; workflows need merge group. Auto-merge: "Allow auto-merge" in Settings, General; off after a push without write access. code owners: dot github slash, root or docs slash; gitignore-style; last match wins.
